idiom_name: hand-written type-descriptor struct with a function-pointer ops table, pointed to by each instance
implementation_notes: C has no class system to lean on, so the whole structure is explicit: a descriptor struct holds the shared data and one function pointer per type-varying operation, and every instance stores a pointer to its descriptor in its first fields. Registration fills a global table keyed by id (loaded from data at startup) and a factory function copies the descriptor's defaults into a fresh instance. This is not an exotic design - CPython's PyTypeObject and GLib/GObject's GTypeClass are exactly this shape: the instance's first member points at a type/class struct whose fields are function pointers and shared data. The classic hand-written form is justified whenever the type set must come from data; for a fixed set of kinds an enum tag plus a switch is simpler and gets compiler checking.
pitfalls: The descriptor must outlive every instance: descriptors allocated on a stack frame or freed by a reload leave dangling 'type' pointers in live instances.
The ops table is untyped at compile time - a function with the wrong signature can be stored in an operation slot and only misbehaves when called; use exact typedefs and never cast.
Nothing enforces registration order: instances created before the registry is populated get NULL or stale descriptors, so creation must fail fast on an unknown id.
